# Attained log-concave target mass on one fixed fiber

Throughout this note d>=1, the inducing set has positive full mixed volume, and
`mu` is its UNNORMALIZED mixed volume, of total mass M. The finitely many
positive-volume integer fibers are denoted `(z_i,K_i)`. Fix one such fiber
`(z_0,K)`.

A finite log-concave measure includes measures on proper affine subspaces,
including positive multiples of point masses. Equivalently, it satisfies
`rho((1-t)A+tB)>=rho(A)^(1-t)rho(B)^t` for compact sets A,B and 0<t<1.
For a nonzero measure this is the usual log-concave-density definition relative
to Lebesgue measure on its affine support. The zero measure is admitted when
taking closures.

Consider

`L(K)=sup{rho(K): rho is finite log-concave, supp(rho) subset K,
                    rho(H)<=mu(H) for every ambient closed halfspace H}`.

All measures on K are identified with measures on the ambient fiber.

## 1. Attainment, including lower-dimensional limits

**Theorem.** The supremum is attained, and

`vol_d(K) <= L(K) <= M`.

**Proof.** Uniform d-volume restricted to K is feasible and log-concave.
All feasible measures have mass at most M, by any ambient halfspace containing
all of S. Measures of mass at most M on compact K are weakly sequentially
compact. For example, diagonal extraction on a countable dense subset of C(K)
produces a bounded positive linear functional, and its representing measure
gives the weak limit. Total mass is continuous in this topology.

Halfspace domination is closed under weak limits, WITHOUT any hypothesis that
boundary hyperplanes have zero mass for the limiting target. Suppose
`rho_j -> rho`. Given `H={w:a.w>=b}` and epsilon>0, put
`G_epsilon={w:a.w>b-epsilon}` and
`H_epsilon={w:a.w>=b-epsilon}`. Portmanteau gives

`rho(H) <= rho(G_epsilon) <= liminf_j rho_j(G_epsilon)
         <= mu(H_epsilon)`.

Let epsilon decrease to zero. Continuity from above for the finite original
measure mu gives `rho(H)<=mu(H)`. This also handles vertical halfspaces whose
boundary contains whole fibers.

Log-concavity is weakly closed. Here is the set-inequality argument. For compact
A,B in the ambient fiber and their open epsilon-neighborhoods A_epsilon and
B_epsilon, let `D=(1-t)A+tB` and let Dbar_epsilon be its closed
epsilon-neighborhood. Then

`(1-t)A_epsilon+tB_epsilon subset Dbar_epsilon`.

The log-concavity inequality extends from compact to open sets by inner
regularity. Therefore

`rho_j(Dbar_epsilon) >= rho_j(A_epsilon)^(1-t)
                       rho_j(B_epsilon)^t`.

The closed-set and open-set parts of Portmanteau imply

`rho(Dbar_epsilon) >= rho(A_epsilon)^(1-t)rho(B_epsilon)^t
                    >= rho(A)^(1-t)rho(B)^t`.

Let epsilon decrease to zero to obtain log-concavity of rho. This proof allows
collapse onto a lower-dimensional affine subspace. A maximizing sequence has
a nonzero limit because every mass is eventually at least vol_d(K)/2.
Mass continuity proves attainment. QED.

No assertion `L(K)>=M/2^n` is made.

## 2. A compact, continuous halfspace capacity on K

Choose R strictly greater than every continuous-coordinate norm occurring in S.
For `u in S^(d-1)` and `t in [-R,R]`, define

`c(u,t)=inf_{a in R^n} sum_i vol_d{x in K_i:
                           a.(z_i-z_0)+u.x>=t}`.

**Lemma.** The infimum is attained by a finite a, and c is continuous on its
compact parameter space.

**Proof.** More generally consider a convergent sequence `(u_j,t_j)->(u,t)`
and arbitrary slope vectors a_j. Extract a subsequence such that every scalar
`a_j.(z_i-z_0)` converges in the extended real line. Let I be the indices with
finite limits s_i. The vector `(s_i)_{i in I}` is in the image of the linear
map `a -> (a.(z_i-z_0))_{i in I}`, because finite-dimensional linear images
are closed. Choose a_0 realizing it.

Project a_j onto the kernel of that linear map. The removed components are
bounded, since their images converge. Thus, on every index outside I, the
projected vectors still have scalar products tending to the prescribed
positive or negative infinity. Choose one projected vector v sufficiently
far along the sequence that all these scalar products have the prescribed
strict signs. It annihilates every `z_i-z_0` with i in I.

For `a=a_0+T v` and sufficiently large finite T, each fiber outside I is
entirely included or entirely excluded, exactly as prescribed by its infinite
limit. Every fiber in I has its prescribed finite threshold exactly. Hence
its cap mass equals the limit of the corresponding masses along the
original sequence. Here we use u!=0 and the fact that d-volume assigns zero
mass to each within-fiber hyperplane. Boundedness of all K_i also justifies
the limits for the infinite thresholds.

Applying this extraction to a minimizing sequence at fixed (u,t) proves
attainment. Applying it to minimizing slopes along `(u_j,t_j)` shows
`c(u,t)<=liminf c(u_j,t_j)`. Conversely c is an infimum of continuous
fixed-slope functions and is therefore upper semicontinuous. Thus it is
continuous. QED.

A measure rho on K is feasible exactly when

`rho{x in K:u.x>=t} <= c(u,t)` for every such (u,t).

Indeed, nonvertical halfspaces normalize to this form. Thresholds below -R
are weaker than the threshold -R because the target cap is already all of K;
thresholds above R have target mass zero. Vertical halfspaces are also
included implicitly. Shrink a vertical halfspace containing K until its
boundary contains z_0. For any fixed unit u and all sufficiently large L,

`L a.(z-z_0)+u.x>=-R`

includes precisely the same integer fibers as that closed vertical
halfspace: fibers on its boundary are all included because R bounds all
continuous coordinates. Consequently the constraint at (u,-R) implies the
vertical one. No irrational-slope approximation or lattice transformation
is used.

## 3. A finite first-order contact certificate

Let rho be a maximizing measure, let W=rho(K)>0, and let
`b=(1/W) integral x d rho` be its barycenter. Let r be the dimension of its
affine support. For each restricted cap
`G=K intersect {u.x>=t}` with rho(G)>0, put

`s_G=log(c(u,t)/rho(G)) >= 0`,
`b_G=(1/rho(G)) integral_G x d rho`.

Define the compact set of asymptotically tight conditional barycenters

`T = intersection_{epsilon>0} closure{b_G:s_G<=epsilon}`.

**Theorem.** T is nonempty and `b in conv(T)`. Consequently there are at most
r+1 points `b_1,...,b_l` of T and nonnegative weights summing to one such that

`b=sum_j theta_j b_j`.

**Proof.** If `inf_G s_G>0`, multiplying rho by a scalar slightly larger than
one preserves every constraint and contradicts maximality. Thus the sets
in the definition of T are nonempty; their compact nested closures give
nonempty compact T.

Suppose b is outside conv(T). Strict affine separation supplies an affine
function ell with `ell(b)>0` and `sup_T ell<0`. Compactness in the definition
of T gives epsilon_0,delta>0 such that

`ell(b_G)<=-delta` whenever `s_G<=epsilon_0`.

Let L bound |ell| on K. Consider the log-concave exponential tilt
`d rho_h = exp(h ell(x)) d rho(x)`, h>0. Multiplication by an exponential of
an affine function preserves log-concavity on the measure's actual affine
support, including the zero-dimensional case.

Uniformly over all caps with rho(G)>0,

`E_{rho|G}[exp(h ell)] <= 1+h ell(b_G)+h^2 L^2 exp(hL)/2`.

For sufficiently small h, this is <=1 on all caps with
`s_G<=epsilon_0`. For the remaining caps it is <=exp(hL)<=exp(epsilon_0),
which is <=exp(s_G). Caps of rho-mass zero remain null. Thus rho_h satisfies
all the capacity constraints and is feasible. But

`rho_h(K) >= W(1+h ell(b)) > W`,

contradicting maximality. Hence b is in conv(T). Caratheodory's theorem in
the r-dimensional affine support gives the stated finite representation.
QED.

This is a necessary finite first-order condition, not a sufficient global
optimality test and not a lower bound for W.

## 4. Actual contacts versus zero-mass limiting contacts

Every point of T can be obtained from a sequence of caps with s_G tending
to zero. Extract convergent parameters `(u_j,t_j)->(u,t)`. Continuity of c
and upper semicontinuity of closed-cap target masses give

`rho(G_j) -> c(u,t) <= rho(G) <= c(u,t)`.

If c(u,t)>0, G is an ACTUAL tight cap and the conditional barycenters converge
to its conditional barycenter. The latter follows from convergence of the
cap masses and the closed-halfspace indicator upper-limit inequality,
applied also to bounded continuous coordinate functions.

If c(u,t)=0, the approximating cap masses vanish. Their conditional
probabilities can converge to a measure on the exposed face

`supp(rho) intersect {u.x=t}`.

Indeed rho(G)=0 forces the support to lie in `{u.x<=t}`, while every weak
limit of these conditional probabilities is supported in G. Such a contact
is not a positive-mass tight halfspace. It must not be silently replaced by
one. The finite certificate above deliberately retains these limiting
contacts.

These statements include lower-dimensional log-concave optimizers and
halfspaces carrying target boundary mass.

## 5. Existence of an actual positive-mass tight ambient halfspace

**Theorem.** Every maximizing rho has at least one ambient closed halfspace H
with `0<rho(H)=mu(H)`.

**Proof.** First suppose the affine support P of rho has positive dimension.
Let delta(x) be the Euclidean distance, within aff(P), from x to the relative
boundary of P. This function is continuous and concave on P: it is the
infimum, over relative unit supporting normals, of the affine support-plane
slacks. It vanishes on the relative boundary, is positive in the relative
interior, and therefore has strictly positive rho-average D.

Suppose for contradiction that no restricted cap is tight with positive mass.
For every sequence of asymptotically tight restricted caps, the compact
capacity parameterization and Section 4 force its conditional probability
limits onto proper exposed boundary faces of P. Hence

`E_{rho|G}[delta] -> 0` as `s_G -> 0`,

uniformly in the sequential sense. Otherwise a counterexample sequence has a
convergent parameter subsequence and a weakly convergent conditional-law
subsequence, contradicting its boundary support.

Choose epsilon with 0<epsilon<D and put phi=delta-epsilon. Then
`E_rho[phi]=D-epsilon>0`, while all sufficiently nearly tight caps have
`E_{rho|G}[phi]<=-epsilon/2`. The bounded concave tilt

`d rho_h=exp(h phi) d rho`

preserves log-concavity. Exactly the uniform Taylor/slack argument in
Section 3 shows it is feasible for sufficiently small h>0, while its total
mass strictly increases. This contradicts maximality.

If P is a single point, every cap of positive target mass has mass W. Any
sequence with s_G tending to zero therefore has capacities tending to W>0.
Section 4 immediately supplies an actual positive-mass tight restricted cap.

In either case, let (u,t) be an actual tight restricted cap. The finite-slope
attainment in Section 2 supplies an ambient halfspace realizing its capacity.
For this halfspace, `rho(H)=c(u,t)=mu(H)>0`. QED.

The other contacts needed in the barycentric certificate may still be
zero-mass limiting contacts. The theorem does not remove them from that
certificate.
